Una cena para contar la experiencia

That morning, at Văcărești, the club collected more than forty bags of rubbish. There was everything: bottles, tins, old shoes, a tyre, a broken plastic chair and even a rusty bicycle that Costel, who had come back from Valencia the day before, insisted on taking home to fix.

Mrs Ecaterina couldn’t bend down, so she took charge of noting down in a notebook everything they found. At the end of the day she read the list out loud, in her translator’s voice, and everyone fell silent. It was a very long list.

“When I was young,” she said afterwards, “there were no plastic bags. We went to the market with a string bag, milk came in bottles that we returned, and bread was wrapped in newspaper. I’m not saying those times were better. But it’s a pity we’ve forgotten some things.”

In the afternoon, Ana came home tired and with black hands. Elena was waiting for her in the garden with Rosa Elena, who was wearing yellow wellies and holding a toy spade. Next to them, on the ground, was a young tree, a metre tall, with its roots wrapped in a sack.
“A walnut tree,” Elena answered. “I bought it at the flower market. Since today is nature day, I thought it was important for the little one to plant her first tree.”

Ana looked towards the bottom of the garden. There, by the fence, was a big old stump, covered in moss, that nobody had ever known what to do with. They had left it there during the renovation because it was too expensive to remove.
“Shall we plant it there, next to the stump?” she asked.
Elena nodded. And then she told her something Ana didn’t know.

That stump was all that was left of the walnut tree that Grandpa Vasile, Elena’s father, had planted on the day she was born. For forty years that tree gave walnuts to the whole family and half the neighbourhood. The children of the street climbed its branches. Mihai, when he was little, broke his arm falling out of it.

“And one summer,” Elena went on, “there was a terrible drought. It didn’t rain for three months. The walnut tree was already very old and didn’t survive. It dried up. Ileana didn’t want to cut it down until there was no other choice. She said it was like cutting off a piece of her husband.”
Ana stared at the stump. Suddenly it looked different to her: it was no longer an old piece of wood getting in the way, but a story.
“It makes sense that Mihai never wanted to remove it,” she said softly.

When Mihai came home from work, he found the three of them digging a hole next to the stump. Well, two of them: Rosa Elena was digging somewhere else, very concentrated, a tiny little hole in which she had put a stone, a leaf and a worm that didn’t look very happy.
Mihai understood at once what they were doing. He didn’t say anything. He took off his jacket, picked up the big spade and started digging with them.
The ground was hard and full of old roots. They had to work for more than an hour. And then, half a metre down, Mihai’s spade struck something metal.

It was a small rusty tin, the kind sweets used to be kept in. Mihai lifted it out carefully and cleaned it with his hand. On the lid you could still just make out the name of a Bucharest sweet factory that no longer existed.

It was very hard to open. When they finally managed it, they found three things inside: a handful of dried walnuts, already black and hard as stones; a folded sheet of paper, yellow and almost transparent with age; and a small metal medal with a faded tricolour ribbon.
Elena took the paper with trembling hands. It was written in Romanian, in pencil, in large, unsteady handwriting, the writing of a man who hadn’t spent long at school.

“For whoever finds this. I planted this walnut tree on the day my daughter was born. I’m putting here the first walnuts and the medal they gave me in the war. I don’t want it in the house. I want the earth to eat it and something good to come out of it. Vasile.”
Nobody spoke for a long time. All you could hear was Rosa Elena, still talking to her worm in a language only she understood.

Ana thought of the old photo Grandpa Gheorghe had given them, with the two young soldiers, him and Vasile, sitting on a rock in uniforms that were too big. She thought of everything that man had never wanted to talk about. And she understood that, however much the war had taken from him, he had decided to give something living back to the earth.
“We have to call Aunt Viorica,” Mihai said at last, his voice breaking. Viorica was Grandpa Vasile’s younger sister, the only one of that generation still alive.
“Tomorrow,” said Elena. “Today we have to finish what he started.”

They put the medal back in the tin, with the walnuts and the letter. Ana added one more thing: the red paper crane, the thousandth, which Rosa Elena always carried in her coat pocket. The little girl protested a bit, but when her granny explained that the crane would look after the tree, she agreed very seriously.

Mihai wrote a new note, in Romanian and Spanish, and put it in the tin too: “The walnut tree was reborn on nature day. It was planted by Rosa Elena, Vasile’s great-granddaughter, with the help of her mother, her father and her granny”.

They buried the tin at the bottom of the hole. On top they put the young walnut tree. Rosa Elena, with her toy spade, threw the first earth over the roots, very slowly, as if she knew it was something important. Then they all helped her finish.

By the time they had finished, night had fallen. Ana watered the tree with Ileana’s old watering can, and the four of them stood looking at it in the light from the kitchen. It was a small, thin tree, almost comical next to the huge moss-covered stump.
“It’ll take about ten years to give walnuts,” said Elena. “I may not see them.”
“Of course you’ll see them, Mum,” said Mihai, putting an arm around her shoulders.

Elena smiled, but said nothing. She looked at the little tree, at the old stump and at her granddaughter, who had fallen asleep standing up, leaning against her legs, with her yellow wellies covered in mud.

That night, Ana wrote in the club’s group chat: “Today we collected forty bags of rubbish and planted a tree. It’s urgent that we look after the planet, yes. But today I learned that it’s just as urgent to look after what those before us left us.” Mrs Ecaterina was the first to reply. She wrote just one word: “Amen”.

The next day, very early, Ana was woken by a noise in the garden. She looked out of the window. It was Mihai, in his pyjamas, with a mug of coffee in his hand, sitting on the old stump next to the new walnut tree. He wasn’t doing anything. He was just looking at the little tree, as if he expected it to grow before his eyes.
Ana went down, sat next to him and took his hand. For a while they sat like that, without speaking, listening to the birds starting to sing in the trees along the street.

“Grandpa used to put me on his shoulders so I could reach the highest walnuts,” Mihai said at last. “I was five. It’s the only thing I remember about him: his huge hands and the smell of walnut leaves. It’s a pity Rosa Elena never knew him.”
“She’ll know him through this tree,” Ana answered. “And you’ll put her on your shoulders so she can reach the highest walnuts.”

Text to read: Aunt Viorica’s message
The next day, Aunt Viorica writes to Ana (Mihai translated the message into Spanish for her).
Dear Ana: I knew nothing about the tin. My brother never told me. It makes sense that he didn’t: he never talked about the war.
I remember the day he planted the walnut tree. It was raining, and he was so happy that he didn’t care about getting wet.
I’m so glad the little one has planted a new one in the same place. It’s as if the story were carrying on.
It’s important that you water it every day in the first year. And when it gives walnuts, keep the first ones for me. I intend to be there to eat them.
